name: Forge-Smith Collective Thermal Cleave 'Ember'
description:
A double-bitted axe with both heads incorporating resistive heating elements that bring the cutting edges to 900 degrees Celsius — hot enough to melt through standard body armor and cauterize flesh on contact, but cool enough to be managed with standard heat-resistant gloves rather than the full thermal protection required by higher-temperature weapons. The Ember represents the Forge-Smith Collective's philosophy of practical lethality: hot enough to work, cool enough to carry.

The weapon's heating elements are powered by a chemical fuel cell integrated into the axe handle — a ferrocerium-based system that ignites on activation and burns steadily for approximately two hours. Unlike electronic heating systems that can be disrupted by EMP or power denial, the Ember's chemical heat source is immune to electronic interference. Once lit, it burns until the fuel is exhausted or the wielder manually vents the reaction chamber.

The double-bitted design serves a practical purpose beyond aesthetics: when one edge loses optimal temperature from repeated contact with cool targets, the wielder rotates to the second edge while the first recovers. In extended engagements, Ember wielders develop a rhythmic alternating pattern — strike, rotate, strike — that maintains consistent thermal cutting performance throughout the fight.
legality: Unlicensed — artisan production, thermal weapon restrictions vary by district
specifications:
head_width: 15 cm per edge (double-bitted)
handle_length: 55 cm
total_weight: 2.2 kg
edge_temperature: 900°C
power_source: Ferrocerium chemical cell, 2 hours continuous
EMP_vulnerability: None — chemical heat source
glove_requirement: Standard heat-resistant
tactical_use: The Ember is a middle-ground thermal weapon — less spectacular than plasma-edge designs but far more practical and sustainable. Its two-hour burn time and EMP immunity make it reliable in the extended, chaotic engagements common in GLMZ's lower tiers. The double-bitted rotation technique allows sustained thermal cutting without performance degradation. Against armored opponents, the 900°C edge softens and melts polymer armor components, creating gaps that subsequent strikes exploit. The weapon's chemical heat signature is visible on thermal imaging, making it poor for stealth — but anyone wielding a double-headed burning axe has already abandoned subtlety.
cultural_context: The Ember has become the Forge-Smith Collective's most recognizable weapon — its burning edges are visible from a distance, and the chemical smell of the ferrocerium fuel is distinctive enough to serve as a warning. Forge-smiths who specialize in thermal axes are called 'brands' within the Collective, and their work is considered a distinct discipline from blade-making. The double-bitted rotation technique has become a recognized martial form, with formal instruction available in lower-tier combat schools.
story_hooks: A batch of Ember fuel cells has been contaminated with an accelerant that causes them to reach 1,600°C — well beyond the axe head's rated temperature. Several wielders have been injured when their weapons partially melted during use. Sabotage or manufacturing error?
An Ember-wielding enforcer has been marking victims with the weapon's hot edge before killing them — a brand in the shape of a specific corporate logo. Someone is sending a message.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist double-bitted thermal axe with a pronounced symmetrical head design. Both cutting edges glow with contained heat, visible as a faint orange corona around the blade tips. The handle tapers from a thick, gripped midsection to a counterbalanced butt. The overall silhouette reads as deliberately functional — no ornamentation, pure purpose.
physical_description.dimensions: Total length: 70 cm (handle 55 cm + head assembly 15 cm); blade width per edge: 15 cm; head depth (front to back): 12 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty but balanced. The 2.2 kg mass distributes evenly across the double-bitted head and reinforced handle, making it manageable for sustained rotational strikes despite the thermal load it carries.
physical_description.primary_material: Hardened steel frame for the head assembly; carbon-composite reinforced polymer for the handle core with steel spine running through the length for structural integrity
physical_description.finish: Battle-worn brushed steel on the axe head with heat-stress discoloration — blues and browns marking the thermal cycling. The handle shows scuffed matte black polymer coating with exposed wear patches revealing raw composite beneath.
physical_description.color_scheme: Steel gray and charcoal black primary; orange-amber heat glow at the blade edges; copper-toned ferrocerium cell casing visible through a reinforced viewport near the handle base
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured rubberized polymer with grooved finger channels; the grip itself is wrapped with thin heat-resistant aramid cord providing additional purchase and thermal dissipation
distinctive_features: Dual cutting edges positioned on opposite sides of the axe head, each independently heated
Visible ferrocerium fuel cell casing at handle base with a small pressure-relief vent
Heat-stress coloration on blade surfaces (oxidized blues and purples from repeated thermal cycling)
Thermal shimmer visible around blade edges when activated
Carved registration marks on the handle for alternating strike position tracking
A small rotation collar at the head junction allowing the wielder to track which edge is 'hot'
Dried cauterized residue (dark brown/black) staining the blade edges from previous use
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: FORGE-SMITH COLLECTIVE stamped in clean sans-serif font on the handle spine, approximately 20 cm from the grip. A serial plate (brushed aluminum) mounted on the lower handle near the fuel cell shows etched production lot number and activation date. The maker's personal mark — a small smith's hammer icon — is hand-engraved near the blade root.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained but clearly field-used. The weapon shows deliberate care in its primary structure but bears the honest scars of repeated thermal cycling and impact. No jury-rigging; this is a tool kept in reliable working condition by someone who understands its value.
